extracted.intended_audience: readers, critics, and poets interested in evaluating and understanding lyric poetry (particularly Wordsworth)
extracted.subtask_description: A close-critical framework for judging poetic quality (as exemplified by Wordsworth), emphasizing diction, imagination, truth to nature, freshness of thought, and moral/intellectual effects of verbal precision. Useful for critics, poets, and students assessing lyric poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strict accuracy of expression / untranslatableness
rubrics_metrics.description: The infallible test of a blameless style: its untranslatableness in words of the same language without injury to the meaning. Include in meaning not only the correspondent object but likewise all the associations which a word recalls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every word's selection and position should be investigated; language should convey object, character, mood, and intentions. In poetry, deliberate choice of every line and phrase makes this attainable. Anti-pattern: loose or vague diction that loses associative nuance; substituting near-synonyms that injure sense or tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction uncorrupted by affectation or misappropriation
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction should be preserved from the affectations and misappropriations which promiscuous authorship and disproportionate reading of contemporary compositions render general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid fashionable or strained turns of phrase; preserve native appropriateness of words. The poet should resist contagion from prevalent bad phraseology (sermons, newspapers, harangues). Example: poetic diction that retains freshness rather than adopting clichéd contemporary locutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Familiarity with masterpieces to form sensitive taste
rubrics_metrics.description: A limited acquaintance with masterpieces suffices to form a correct and sensitive taste, whereas wide acquaintance only with tasteless or perverted works leads to contagion of bad taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate reading of true masters; limit exposure to popular but poor exemplars. Educational implication: guide young readers toward high exemplars to form taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education in verbal analysis (habit of investigating words)
rubrics_metrics.description: From boyhood, investigating the meaning of every word and the reason of its choice and position trains the judgment and familiarizes one with logic and precision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teaching writers/children to examine word choice develops judgment: it is both moral and intellectual training. Pedagogic note: deliberate verbal analysis yields lasting habits of accurate thinking and expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Veracity and mental accuracy via verbal precision
rubrics_metrics.description: Veracity (truthfulness of thought and character) is closely connected with habits of mental accuracy; verbal precision helps preclude fanaticism which exploits indistinct watch-words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear, precise language limits rhetorical manipulation and vague dogmatism. Anti-pattern: reliance on indistinct slogans or watch-words that inflame feeling without thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivation of judgment: distinguishing similar from the same
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful judgment depends on distinguishing what is peculiar in a thing from what it has in common with others, so as to select the most probable instead of the merely possible or positively unfit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A critic or poet should aim for the most appropriate, probable expression and interpretation, not merely possible ones. This is a general epistemic/scholarly criterion linked to careful wording and choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perspicuity to the intended audience (fit audience find)
rubrics_metrics.description: A poem is not necessarily obscure because it does not aim to be popular; it is enough if a work be perspicuous to those for whom it is written: 'Fit audience find, though few.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess clarity relative to intended readership. High or arduous poetry may rightly be limited in audience; criterion is intelligibility to the appropriate, accustomed reader rather than mass popularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and weight of thoughts and sentiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Thoughts and sentiments should have correspondent weight and sanity — won from the poet’s own meditative observation rather than borrowed from books; they should be fresh and possess the dew upon them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value reflections that feel native and meditative, not secondhand. Even in minor pieces, just and original reflection enhances value. Anti-pattern: ideas that read as mere literary commonplace or learned ornament without living source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sinewy strength and originality of single lines/paragraphs (curiosa felicitas)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent 'curiosa felicitas' — felicitous turns of diction and striking, original lines and paragraphs — contribute distinctive excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Single-line/paragraph-level felicities (unexpected apt phrasing, compressed power) are a mark of high poetic skill. Critics should note memorable, concentrated passages as evidence of craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth of nature in images and descriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Perfect truth of nature in images and descriptions as taken immediately from nature, showing long and genial intimacy with the spirit of nature; images distinguished only by greater softness and lustre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetic description should not falsify or distort but reveal veins and tints overlooked by common observation. Assess accuracy and fidelity to the observed natural world and the poet’s ability to elevate ordinary detail into gem-like images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meditative pathos and sympathetic contemplation
rubrics_metrics.description: A union of deep and subtle thought with sensibility: a sympathy with man as man, more contemplative than fellow-suffering, able to read the human face beneath circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value a calm, philosophic pathos that dignifies common humanity and preserves the Creator's image amid suffering. Examples: poems that move readers to tears through quiet, contemplative insight rather than sensationalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imaginative power (highest, strict sense)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet’s gift of Imagination — the ability to 'add the gleam, the light that never was' — a creative consecration and original vision akin in power (if not mode) to Shakespeare and Milton.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imagination may produce likenesses that are strange or recondite; it is not always graceful as mere fancy but is judged by its capacity to transform thought and object into a new, consecrated vision. Anti-pattern: mere ornamenting fancy without imaginative synthesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of fancy vs imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Fancy (play of images) and Imagination are distinct: fancy may be occasionally ungraceful or too strange, whereas Imagination, in the strict sense, is the creative power that unites and consecrates thought and object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should distinguish between superficial fancifulness and deep imaginative synthesis; penalize gratuitous strangeness that lacks transformative insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resistance to contemporary corrupt eloquence (antidote of style)
rubrics_metrics.description: In an age of corrupt eloquence, a watchful, strict accuracy of expression is both proper food for the understanding and an antidote to prevailing bad style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a poet’s style combats contemporary affectations and offers corrective exemplars. Educational and moral value of style counts alongside aesthetic value.
